blocks.text: Many endocrine glands are controlled by the master gland, the pituitary, but the pituitary is itself controlled by part of the brain, the hypothalamus. The hypothalamus has neurosecretory cells, which conduct nerve impulses and also secrete hormones.

items: Control of the posterior pituitary: oxytocin and ADH are made by neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus; their axons carry the hormones to the posterior pituitary, where they are stored for release into the blood.

Control of the anterior pituitary: blood vessels connect the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary. Neurosecretory cells release hormones that travel through these vessels: releasing hormones make the anterior pituitary make and secrete its hormones, and inhibiting hormones stop it.

blocks.alt: Section of the hypothalamus and pituitary. Neurosecretory cells (orange stars) lie in the hypothalamus. Axons of most run down the stalk into the posterior pituitary; a few end at a capillary bed at the top of the stalk. An artery feeds that capillary bed and the anterior pituitary; a portal vessel runs from the stalk capillaries to capillaries in the anterior pituitary. Another artery enters the posterior pituitary; veins from both lobes join below.
